You can inspect later, but **finding problems after the option period does not itself give you a right to cancel**. [Inspection guidance](https://www.texasrealestate.com/legal-and-ethics/legal-resources/legal-faqs/as-is-and-inspections)

For **Manchester, England**, the usual route is **offer accepted → legal checks, survey and mortgage → exchange of contracts → completion and keys**. Your solicitor handles the legal purchase; you arrange finance and a survey.

[Assumption] You’re buying through a normal private sale. Auctions, new builds and shared ownership can have different commitments and deadlines.

**Your next three steps**

1. **You: instruct a solicitor experienced in leasehold flats.** If using a mortgage, confirm they’re on your lender’s panel. Get a written quote covering leasehold work, searches, registration, management-company fees and any building-safety work.
2. **You and your lender/broker: progress the mortgage and budget.** Allow for legal costs, survey, any Stamp Duty Land Tax, moving costs and ongoing flat charges.
3. **You: arrange an independent survey.** The lender’s valuation serves the lender and does not replace your survey. Ask what the survey will cover about the wider building and communal areas. [GOV.UK buying guide](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/how-to-buy-a-home/how-to-buy)

**What your solicitor should handle**

Ask them to confirm these points in their written report before exchange:

| Area | What you need them to establish |
|---|---|
| **Ownership and title** | The seller can sell; the legal plan matches the flat, parking and storage you expect; access and communal rights are adequate. |
| **Searches and enquiries** | Relevant local-authority, drainage and environmental searches; any additional location-specific searches; satisfactory replies about alterations, permissions and disputes. |
| **Lease** | Years remaining, ground rent and increases, repair responsibilities, restrictions on alterations, pets or letting, and implications for mortgageability and resale. |
| **Building finances** | Management pack, service-charge accounts and budget, reserve fund, arrears, disputes, planned major works and consultation notices. Clarify your potential liability for later bills. |
| **Building safety** | Relevant fire/cladding documents, remediation plans and funding, whether statutory leaseholder protections apply, and whether the lender accepts the position. |
| **Contract and mortgage** | Explain obligations and unresolved risks, satisfy lender requirements, agree the exchange deposit and completion date, and obtain your authority to exchange. |
| **Completion and afterwards** | Transfer purchase funds, deal with the applicable SDLT return/payment, register the purchase and mortgage, and serve required leasehold notices. |

These leasehold checks matter even if the flat comes with a “share of freehold”. [Leasehold Advisory Service](https://www.lease-advice.org/buying-and-selling/leasehold-property/things-to-know/), [SRA conveyancing scope](https://www.sra.org.uk/solicitors/guidance/transparency-in-price-and-service/)

**When you become committed**

In an ordinary English private sale, an accepted offer is not legally binding; **exchange of contracts is the binding point**. Signing paperwork in preparation is not itself exchange. Resolve material survey, finance, lease and building-safety questions first. Completion is when the balance is paid and you receive the keys. [GOV.UK](https://www.gov.uk/buying-a-home/transferring-ownership)

There’s no transaction-specific deadline available yet. Ask your solicitor to track mortgage-offer expiry, any reservation deadline and the agreed completion date.

**Human check**

- **Solicitor:** confirm legal risks, building liabilities and lender requirements before exchange.
- **Surveyor:** assess physical condition and identify any specialist investigations needed before commitment.
- **You:** decide whether the total costs and restrictions are acceptable; verify bank details through a trusted telephone number before transferring money.

Assuming you’re buying through an ordinary private sale, Manchester follows the **England conveyancing process**. Your solicitor handles the legal purchase; you arrange the finance and survey. For a flat, the lease, building’s finances and fire safety position deserve particular attention.

If you’ve already had an offer accepted, start at step 2.

1. **Agree the purchase.** Make your offer “subject to contract” and clarify what’s included, whether the seller has a chain, and whether the flat will be empty on completion. An accepted offer is generally not legally binding until contracts are exchanged.

2. **Appoint your solicitor and arrange finance.** Choose someone experienced in leasehold flats and, where relevant, building safety work. If you’re borrowing, confirm they’re on your mortgage lender’s panel. Get a written quote including leasehold extras, searches, registration, tax and management-company fees. Provide ID and evidence of your deposit’s source promptly.

3. **Arrange a survey while the legal checks proceed.** Your solicitor investigates ownership, searches and documents, raises questions with the seller’s solicitor, and checks mortgage conditions. You commission an appropriate survey: a lender’s valuation is not a substitute for checking the flat’s condition. For a flat, establish how far the survey covers the wider building. [Government buying guide](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/how-to-buy-a-home/how-to-buy)

4. **Review everything before exchange.** Read your solicitor’s written report and resolve material questions. Have your mortgage offer, survey findings, deposit and completion funds ready. Agree the completion date and confirm the building’s insurance arrangements.

5. **Exchange contracts.** Your solicitor exchanges with your authority and arranges the contractual deposit. **This is the binding commitment**; withdrawing afterwards can have substantial financial consequences.

6. **Complete and register.** Your solicitor transfers the purchase money; you receive the keys. They then handle the Stamp Duty Land Tax return/payment as applicable, Land Registry application and necessary leasehold notices. [Conveyancing process](https://www.gov.uk/buying-a-home/transferring-ownership), [exchange and completion](https://www.moneyhelper.org.uk/en/homes/buying-a-home/contract-exchange-completion-when-buying-a-home)

For the flat itself, ask your solicitor to cover these points explicitly:

| Check | What you need explained |
|---|---|
| **Ownership and lease** | Tenure, years remaining, extension implications, and any terms affecting mortgageability or resale. “Share of freehold” still usually involves a lease. |
| **What you’re buying** | Lease plan, parking, balcony, storage, access rights, and responsibility for windows, roof and structural repairs. |
| **Ground rent and restrictions** | Rent increases; rules on letting, pets, alterations and use; whether previous alterations had the required consents. |
| **Building finances** | Management pack, recent service-charge accounts and current budget, reserve fund, arrears, disputes and insurance. |
| **Major works** | Planned or proposed roof, lift, façade or other works, Section 20 consultation notices, likely contribution and who pays outstanding liabilities. |
| **Searches and permissions** | Local authority, drainage and environmental searches; address-specific flood or historic mining checks where appropriate; relevant planning and building-control documents. |

These are core leasehold enquiries. Ask for an explanation of the risks and likely costs, alongside copies of the documents. [LEASE’s buying checklist](https://www.lease-advice.org/buying-and-selling/leasehold-property/things-to-know/)

**Building safety needs a separate, clear answer.** Your solicitor should establish whether there are cladding or other fire safety defects, proposed remediation, confirmed funding and any potential costs to you. Where applicable, they should examine the leaseholder deed of certificate and landlord’s certificate and explain whether statutory cost protections attach to the flat. An EWS1 may be relevant to your lender, but is not universally required and does not settle every safety or liability question. [Government protections guidance](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/leaseholder-protections-on-building-safety-costs-in-england-frequently-asked-questions), [RICS EWS1 guidance](https://www.rics.org/news-insights/current-topics-campaigns/fire-safety/cladding-external-wall-system-ews-faqs)

A useful instruction to give your solicitor is: **“Before exchange, please explain in writing any unresolved issues affecting my costs, use of the flat, mortgage or ability to sell.”**

No. **Zero DOB violations and zero permits do not establish that the finished basement is legal.** No violations may simply mean no violation has been recorded. No permits could mean work was done without required permits, records are incomplete, or the search missed the property’s records.

“Fully finished in 2015” is a marketing claim, not proof of approval. Also, a basement approved as accessory space is different from one legally approved for sleeping or as a separate apartment. Whether NYC classifies the space as a basement or a cellar matters.

Before relying on the listing:

- Check both **DOB BIS and DOB NOW**, using the property’s correct borough, block and lot.
- Review the **Certificate of Occupancy, approved plans, and any required permits and final sign-offs** for the renovation. Some older buildings legitimately lack a Certificate of Occupancy, so that absence alone is not decisive.
- Ask the seller for documentation establishing the basement’s approved use.
- Have a NYC architect or engineer compare the actual layout and intended use with those records, and have your attorney review the issue before you commit.

**Treat its legality as unverified until the records and physical conditions support the claimed use.**

**Yes. Both are must-resolve issues before signing, although neither automatically means you should abandon the house.** I’m relying on your descriptions, not the actual deed or contract. State and city are unknown, so this is general U.S. guidance.

**1. Seller names and the life estate**

[document, as reported] Jane Roe and Mark Poe are the sellers. [record, as reported] Alice Roe appears as owner, with a retained life estate in a 2009 deed.

An innocent explanation is that Jane and Mark received the *remainder interest*, meaning ownership after Alice’s life estate ends. The deed you describe makes that plausible; it does not establish their identities or current authority. The ownership database may also be outdated. [Explanation of life estates](https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/life_estate).

The concern is whether they can deliver **full ownership free of Alice’s life estate**, rather than only their future interest. Ask your attorney:

> “Please confirm who holds each current ownership interest under the 2009 deed and subsequent records, and Jane and Mark’s capacity to sell. If Alice is living, what signature or valid release is required? If deceased, what proof does the title insurer require? Please confirm we will receive full title without a life-estate exception.”

Have the attorney/title company review the actual deed, later recordings, and any claimed power of attorney or estate authority. A name mismatch alone does not prove fraud or invalidate the transaction.

**2. Paragraph 22 gives up a meaningful protection**

[document, as reported] Paragraph 22 acknowledges an adequate testing opportunity and waives it. This may be routine form language, but **routine does not mean harmless**. It is not evidence that testing happened or that the home is lead-safe.

For most pre-1978 U.S. housing, federal rules provide a 10-day opportunity for a lead inspection or risk assessment before becoming obligated, unless changed by agreement or waived in writing. Waiving testing does not erase applicable seller disclosure duties. [EPA disclosure requirements](https://www.epa.gov/lead/real-estate-disclosures-about-potential-lead-hazards).

A 1925 construction date, as you report, does not prove a current hazard. But with children planned, I would favor a **certified lead inspection and risk assessment before accepting that waiver**. Paint testing identifies lead; risk assessment evaluates hazards such as dust and deteriorating paint. Renovation can create hazardous dust, including when preparing a nursery. [EPA guidance](https://www.epa.gov/lead/reduce-risk-lead-exposure-home).

Ask your attorney:

> “Please confirm paragraph 22’s effect and whether we can replace it with a testing period, access, and an explicit right to cancel with deposit return if results are unacceptable. Please also confirm receipt of required lead disclosures and existing reports.”

**Human check**

- **Attorney/title company:** resolve ownership and required signatures before you sign; verify clear title before closing.
- **Certified lead professional and buyer:** assess hazards and likely management work before waiving testing.
- **If already signed:** contact your attorney promptly about remaining deadlines and amendment options. Do not assume a fresh 10-day period or stop contractual performance on your own.

Yes. **The ownership mismatch and the lead-paint waiver both need attention before you sign or close.** Neither proves the deal is defective, but the facts you gave leave important questions unresolved.

**Who can convey the property?** The 2009 deed may have transferred the remainder interest to Jane and Mark while Alice retained a life estate, meaning a right to possess the property during her lifetime. Public records listing Alice alone may not tell the full story.

- If Alice is alive and still holds that interest, Jane and Mark generally cannot convey full ownership free of it without her joining in the conveyance or a valid release.
- If Alice has died, the title company will typically need acceptable proof that the life estate ended.
- Have your real-estate attorney and title company review the actual recorded deed, later recordings, and title commitment. Ask them to confirm **who must sign to deliver clear, insurable title and possession at closing**.

**Paragraph 22 may surrender a valuable lead inspection right.** A 1925 house presents a meaningful possibility of lead-based paint. Deteriorating paint and dust from windows, doors, or renovations are particular concerns for young children and during pregnancy.

For most sales of pre-1978 housing, federal rules require sellers to provide known lead information, available reports, and the EPA pamphlet, and offer a 10-day inspection opportunity unless the parties agree otherwise in writing. Buyers can waive that opportunity. **Waiving inspection does not eliminate the seller’s disclosure obligations, and disclosure does not establish that the house is lead-free.**

Ask your attorney to revise paragraph 22 to preserve a lead inspection/risk-assessment contingency, with enough time to receive results and a clear right to cancel or negotiate remediation. A routine home inspection usually does not include this assessment; use a certified lead professional. If you already signed, contact your attorney promptly about deadlines and whether the seller will agree to restore that right.

- **Time:** One skilled person replacing a crew can extend the project, adding housing and carrying costs.

Ask for the $300,000 quote broken into materials, labor by trade, subcontractors, and contractor overhead/profit. Then price what remains after your dad’s specific contribution, including travel, tools, helpers, and contingency. **Until that budget is verified, treat the savings as upside, especially if the purchase only works financially at $150,000.**

**Treat the listing’s “bedroom” label as unverified until you check both the room and its approval records.** [document, as you described it] A showing can identify problems, but cannot establish legal bedroom status.

For **Columbus, Ohio**, I don’t have a local code reference in the housing skills, so this is a screening checklist. Have the building department confirm the requirements and any existing-house exceptions for that address.

Bring a tape measure, flashlight and phone. Focus on:

- **Escape directly from the room.** Look for an operable exterior escape window or exterior door. Don’t assume the basement stairs or a window in another room qualifies. With permission, open the window fully and measure the actual unobstructed opening’s width and height, plus the height from the finished floor to the opening. Photograph these measurements.
- **The outside escape route.** Inspect the window well’s width, projection and depth, any ladder or steps, and whether the window opens fully. Check whether covers, bars, a deck or stored items obstruct escape. Note whether release requires a key or tool.
- **Ceiling height and room size.** Measure finished floor to ceiling, separately under beams and ducts, and record room length and width. Photos and listing dimensions are insufficient.
- **Habitable conditions.** Look for permanent heat, ventilation, a smoke alarm, nearby carbon-monoxide protection, and a usable route to the stairs. Note musty odors, water stains, damp carpet and standing water in the window well. Ask for water-intrusion history and radon results.

**Ask the agent:**

> “Please provide the approved basement plans identifying this room as a bedroom or sleeping room, the permit number, and passed final inspection records. When was it converted?”

[record] Columbus provides a [permit search portal](https://portal.columbus.gov/CA/Welcome.aspx) and [records-request process](https://www.columbus.gov/Business-Development/Building-Zoning-Services/Records-Research). An older approval may explain a room that differs from today’s standards, but that needs documentary confirmation. An empty online search proves neither approval nor a violation.

Also have your lender/appraiser confirm how the basement bedroom and below-grade area will be reported and valued.

**Human check**

- **You:** record measurements and photographs, including exactly where ceiling heights were taken.
- **Inspector and local building department:** assess safety and confirm approved sleeping use, applicable dimensions and exceptions.
- **You and your agent:** resolve this before your inspection contingency expires; don’t rely on the room as a bedroom until confirmed.

**Check the escape route and the permit record first.** A finished room with a bed does not establish that it’s an approved bedroom. Bring a tape measure and take photos.

1. **Open the bedroom’s escape window.** Normally, the room itself needs an emergency opening directly outdoors, such as a qualifying window or exterior door. Stairs upstairs or a window in another basement room generally won’t substitute. Ohio has a limited sprinkler exception.

   For a window, measure the **actual unobstructed opening when open**, not the glass or frame:
   
   - At least **20 inches wide** and **24 inches high**.
   - At least **5 square feet for below-grade or grade-floor openings**; otherwise **5.7 square feet**. A 20-by-24-inch opening is too small.
   - Sill no more than **44 inches above the finished floor**.
   - Opens from inside without keys, tools, or special knowledge.

   A window well needs at least **9 square feet**, with width and outward projection each at least **36 inches**. Wells deeper than **44 inches** need a permanent ladder or steps. Check that the window opens fully and any cover releases from inside. [Ohio residential code, §310](https://codes.ohio.gov/assets/laws/administrative-code/rules/4101/8/4101%248-3-01_eff_7_1_19.pdf)

2. **Measure the room and look for basic habitability.** Ohio’s baseline is **70 square feet**, **7 feet in each horizontal dimension**, and generally a **7-foot ceiling**, with limited obstruction exceptions. Check permanent heat, light, ventilation, and smoke alarms inside and immediately outside the bedroom. [Ohio residential code, §§303–305 and 314](https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-4101:8-3-01)

3. **Look for basement problems.** Check for musty smells, water stains, damp carpet, pooled water in the window well, and a route to the stairs that passes through a furnace room. Columbus has additional basement occupancy requirements covering dampness, windows, access, and equipment separation. Have the city confirm their application to this room; the available [local fair-housing guide reproduces §4541.04](https://www.cofha.com/rental/files/2018%20Fair%20Housing%20and%20Non-discriminatory%20Rental%20Practices.PDF), but is dated.

4. **Ask for proof of bedroom approval.** Request the basement permit number, approved floor plan showing **bedroom/sleeping room**, and passed final inspections. A permit for a recreation room doesn’t establish approval for sleeping. Columbus requires a permit and plan review to finish a basement. [City permit requirements](https://www.columbus.gov/files/sharedassets/city/v/2/building-and-zoning/document-library/typical-residential-projects-2026.pdf)

Before relying on the advertised bedroom count, have your inspector assess it and verify the records with **Columbus Building and Zoning Services, 614-645-7433**. Confirm the actual jurisdiction first: a Columbus mailing address may be served by another building department. Ask the agent and lender separately how the below-grade bedroom and square footage will be reported and valued.
